extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and beginning newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom exercises and editing guidance for reporting, rewriting, and critiquing news stories across beats (death notices, fires, society, sports, localizing dispatches, handling refusals, combining bulletins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Death notice reporting details
rubrics_metrics.description: Time and place of death, yesterday at the New York hospital; age, 36; occupation, sexton at Christ Church on West Thirty-sixth Street; attending physician, Dr. Henry Adair; cause of death, swallowing false teeth while at breakfast with his wife yesterday; efforts to save him: Dr. Adair summoned immediately, incision made in throat, silver tube inserted to allow passage of air to the lungs, and operation later at hospital. Patient failed to rally after operation. Survivors: wife and two children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a death story include the key factual elements listed above — exact time and place, age, occupation, attending physician, cause of death, detailed efforts to save the person (medical interventions and timeline), and survivors. These items form the factual core of the lead and body of the obituary/death notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire/accident incident reporting details
rubrics_metrics.description: Date, to-day, April 19, at 4:30 a.m.; location, 1516 Orleans Street, Chicago; cause of fire, supposedly crossed wires on second floor where fire started; loss $60,000 according to C. M. Holmes, Jr., manager of the scientific department; persons injured, one fireman slightly injured by falling glass; institutions whose diplomas were destroyed, George Washington University, Grinnell College, University of North Dakota, Marquette University, Dakota Wesleyan College; lives endangered, five firemen who were climbing a ladder on the rear wall when it fell; insurance, amount not obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise time/date and address, suspected cause, estimated monetary loss and source of estimate, injuries, institutions or property affected, any lives endangered, and insurance status. These details should appear early and be attributed to named sources when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society/wedding reporting checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: For engagement and wedding items include: full names and ages of bride/groom; parents' names and occupations; home addresses; bridegroom's occupation (e.g., cashier, bank); history of acquaintanceship; wedding date and time; church name and officiant (Rev. C. K. Tanner); who will give the bride away; best man and maid of honor names; bridesmaids/flower girls names; any heirloom or special gown detail (old Brussels lace worn by mother); predominant color scheme; number of invitations issued; luncheon/reception time and immediate plans (honeymoon, temporary residence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise social details that readers expect in society columns — who, when, where, attire details and notable heirlooms, attendants, invitations, and post-ceremony plans. These facts form the core of short society items and should be organized clearly (lead with the most newsworthy or locally relevant fact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine bulletins/updates with earlier stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bulletin arrives after a morning dispatch (e.g., confession and subsequent suicide of a suspect, discovery of a note, inquest scheduled, funeral times), combine the new bulletin with the earlier morning story into a single coherent update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate new developments into the existing narrative by (1) inserting the bulletin information near the top with clear timestamps, (2) preserving chronological order, (3) attributing sources (coroner, sheriff), and (4) adding concrete follow-up details such as inquest and funeral arrangements. Avoid duplication and make clear what is new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localizing a national or out-of-town dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Write up material (e.g., George Ade's speech) for a local paper by stressing the local connection: George Ade's home is in Indiana — angle the story for an Indianapolis morning paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find and lead with the local tie or angle that makes a broader item relevant to your paper's readership (home town, local speakers or attendees, local implications). Tailor quotations and context to emphasize why readers locally should care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct quotes, attributions, and attendee lists
rubrics_metrics.description: In banquet/speech accounts include direct quotations (e.g., Mr. Whitlock on 'American Ideals'), who introduced the speaker, who presided, and notable attendees with names and roles (e.g., Dr. M. Woolsey Stryker, M. A. Van der Vyede, Nathaniel C. Wright).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exact quoted language where it illuminates the subject, identify speakers, and give a brief list of prominent attendees and their relevance. Attribute opinions and judgments (e.g., praise for Whitlock) to the speaker or introducer rather than presenting them as the paper's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling refusal to be interviewed / 'not at home' situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting example: a subject is 'not at home' to reporters; reporter rings doorbell, maid refuses, reporter calls by telephone and confirms refusal. The scenario tests whether the story is meritorious or blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When refused access, reporters should (a) record attempts (knock, ask who is calling), (b) attempt reasonable follow-up (telephone), (c) avoid assuming guilt or evasiveness without evidence, and (d) evaluate newsworthiness: if refusal itself is newsworthy (e.g., in charge of large public funds), report the refusal with attributed facts rather than innuendo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing obituaries and weekly-paper death notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show poor obituary copy: overly wordy and euphemistic phrasing, imprecise age dates, family/relationship confusion, irrelevant color commentary (e.g., 'worked as busy as a bee').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite obituaries to be factual and concise: state birth and death dates/ages clearly, marital status and survivors, place and cause of death, funeral arrangements, and omit florid language and irrelevant anecdotes unless they are essential human-interest facts. Ensure grammatical clarity and chronological coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporting: accuracy over florid opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The provided baseball story is an example of excessive, insulting, and clichéd copy (overwrought metaphors, hyperbole, moralizing asides). It recounts the game's events but buries them under sarcasm and unrelated conceits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sports stories concentrate on the factual game elements (score, key plays, errors, pitching changes, turning points), use a clear lead summarizing outcome, and avoid excessive sarcasm, gratuitous insults, and metaphors that obscure facts. Rewrites should strengthen weak points by tightening language, clarifying chronology, and focusing on play-by-play significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting 'almost excellent' pieces: identify and fix the single grave weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: A human-interest piece about a boy and his lamb is called 'almost excellent' but 'has one grave weakness.' The exercise asks the student to rewrite, strengthening weak points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising, identify the principal flaw (e.g., weak or absent lead, muddled chronology, unbalanced tone, missing context) and correct it: craft a stronger lead, tighten narrative order, remove irrelevant detail, preserve human interest without sensationalism, and make cause-and-effect clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice across beats and special assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Special assignments suggested: reporting sermons, local addresses, commercial banquets, football/basketball/baseball games, weather forecast stories, society items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should practice a variety of beats to learn different conventions: sermon reports (capture gist and notable quotes), banquet coverage (attendees and speeches), weather (today's account and forecast), and sports (see sports criteria). Each beat has its own facts-to-include checklist and conventional lead structures; use exercises to master them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on a 'collection of adjectives' and show, don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: An early anecdote notes the journalist 'requires only a collection of adjectives' sarcastically, warning against dressing copy with adjectives rather than facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete facts, precise details, and vivid specific actions over vague adjectives and generalizing epithets. Let reporting and documented quotes supply color; avoid padding with gratuitous descriptors that weaken credibility and clarity.
